title: The galactic centre
caption: The centre of the Milky Way, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Galactic Centre, Sagittarius A* · constellation Sagittarius · about 27000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This infrared image from Hubble looks toward the centre of our own galaxy, the Milky Way, 27,000 light-years from Earth. In ordinary visible light, this region is hidden behind thick clouds of dust.

Infrared light can slip through that dust, which is why astronomers used Hubble's infrared capabilities to peer into the region. What they see is a nuclear star cluster, a dense crowd of stars packed around the very middle of the galaxy.

At the centre of that cluster, and of the frame, lies the Milky Way's supermassive black hole, known as Sagittarius A*. A supermassive black hole is an object so dense that not even light can escape it, and one of these is thought to sit at the heart of most large galaxies. The black hole itself cannot be seen, but the crowded stars around it show how crowded our galaxy's core is.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (6.47 x 5.59 arcminutes) and distance (27000 light years), the frame spans roughly 51 × 44 light-years. Its light set out about 27,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using three infrared filters. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
filters: 1.532 μm · Infrared H2O and NH3 (Hubble WFC3)
understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the eye, and in visible light dust blocks our view of this region almost completely.
